theme: The LORD reigns; let the earth rejoice
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 97. You will read it again later in the plan. Read it now as the answer to Obadiah: the LORD reigns, and pride cannot stand before him.
settingTheScene: Psalm 97 is a royal psalm, one of a group (Psalms 93, 95 to 99) that begin or center on “The LORD reigns.” Coming after Obadiah’s judgment on proud Edom, it celebrates God’s rule, which terrifies the proud and delights the righteous. The returned community, small and surrounded by hostile neighbors, sang it as a reminder of who is really in charge.
observation: “The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad!” (v. 1).
“Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne” (v. 2).
“Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries all around” (v. 3).
“The mountains melt like wax before the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth” (v. 5).
“The heavens declare his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory” (v. 6).
“All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols” (v. 7).
“The LORD loves those who hate evil; he preserves the lives of his saints” (v. 10).
“Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” (v. 11).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with joy: the reign of God is good news for the whole earth, even the distant coastlands. This is a striking claim. The one who rules is not a distant tyrant but the one on whose throne “righteousness and justice” rest. His reign is moral. It means that the world is not left to chance or to the powerful.

But his presence is awesome. Clouds and thick darkness, fire, lightning, and melting mountains. These are the images of Sinai. They remind the readers that God is holy. The imagery says that no one can approach him without fear unless he provides a way.

The effect on idols is immediate. “All worshipers of images are put to shame.” Even the so-called gods bow down before him. This is the same truth you saw in Psalm 115, and Obadiah’s warning to Edom. The proud who trust in themselves, in their strongholds, in their false gods will be shamed.

Yet the psalm is not only about terror. Zion hears and is glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoice. The judgments of God are matters for gladness among his people because they mean that wrongs will be set right. And then the psalm gives instruction: “O you who love the LORD, hate evil.” Love and hate are linked. Loving the good means rejecting what destroys it. And God “preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked.”

The last two verses contain a beautiful promise: “Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.” The image is of a seed planted in darkness that will rise as light. Those who walk uprightly may seem to sow in sorrow, but God has sown light for them. In the end, the psalm tells us to rejoice in the LORD and give thanks to his holy name.
connection: Revelation 19:6: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.” Hebrews 1:6 quotes verse 7: “Let all God’s angels worship him.” John 8:12: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” Romans 12:9: “Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.” Matthew 5:14-16 says we are the light of the world. Isaiah 9:2: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
application:
Say aloud, “The LORD reigns,” when you feel anxious about the world.

Ask what it means to “hate evil” in a way that is tender toward people.

Receive the promise: “Light is sown for the righteous.” Trust that your faithfulness is not wasted.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you rejoice that he reigns.
Ask him to shame the idols you are tempted by.
Thank him for preserving the lives of his saints.
